routes.title: From a polynomial to its Galois group
routes.audience: A first course in field theory
routes.goal: Prove irreducibility and determine the Galois group from its permutation action.
routes.checkpoint: For \(f(x)=x^5-x-1\), prove \(\operatorname{Gal}(f/\mathbb Q)=S_5\) and state what each prime contributes.

steps.title: Fields, irreducibility, and Galois actions
steps.note: Fix the ground field, distinguish irreducibility from separability, and relate factorization to the action on roots.

steps.title: Reduction modulo primes
steps.note: Use one finite-field factorization or intersect the factor degrees permitted by several primes. Examine why this method can be inconclusive for an irreducible polynomial.

steps.title: Frobenius and factorization modulo primes
steps.note: At a prime of good reduction, a squarefree factorization gives a cycle type in the global Galois group. Group-theoretic criteria then restrict the possible groups.

steps.title: Transitivity, primitivity, and cycle criteria
steps.note: Apply block systems, transpositions, and long-cycle criteria to permutations obtained from local arithmetic.

steps.title: Discriminants, parity, and ramification
steps.note: The discriminant detects repeated roots. For a separable polynomial in characteristic zero, its square class determines the sign character of the root action, but does not determine the group.

steps.title: Exercise
steps.note: For \(f(x)=x^5-x-1\), prove \(\operatorname{Gal}(f/\mathbb Q)=S_5\) and state what each prime contributes.

routes.title: From valuations to large groups
routes.audience: Readers comfortable with valuations and finite permutation groups
routes.goal: Use coefficient divisibility to restrict factor degrees and obtain long prime cycles.
routes.checkpoint: Separate the irreducibility input, the Newton-polygon input, Jordan's theorem, and the discriminant step.

steps.title: Schönemann–Eisenstein and Dumas criteria
steps.note: Coefficient divisibility can exclude every proper factor degree. Translation and Newton-polygon slopes extend the elementary criterion.

steps.title: Newton polygons and Galois groups
steps.note: Determine p-adic root valuations, combine factor-degree restrictions, and use suitable prime divisors of slope denominators to force large groups.

steps.title: Transitivity, primitivity, and cycle criteria
steps.note: Apply block systems, transpositions, and long-cycle criteria to permutations obtained from local arithmetic.

steps.title: Taylor polynomials
steps.note: Compare exponential truncations, with alternating or symmetric groups, and geometric truncations, whose factors are cyclotomic.

steps.title: Generalized Laguerre polynomials
steps.note: Use factorial coefficient products to relate local slopes to Galois-group constraints. Distinguish fixed parameter with increasing degree from fixed degree with varying parameter.

steps.title: Exercise
steps.note: Separate the irreducibility input, the Newton-polygon input, Jordan's theorem, and the discriminant step.

routes.title: Irreducibility and Galois groups in families
routes.audience: Researchers moving from examples to a family theorem
routes.goal: Identify forced factors and symmetries, then determine the ambient permutation group.
routes.checkpoint: State the normalization, the ambient permutation group, a proved result, and an unresolved question with its source and stated range.

steps.title: Reciprocal polynomials
steps.note: For a reciprocal polynomial of even degree, form the trace polynomial of half the degree. Study the remaining quadratic extensions to determine irreducibility and the Galois group.

steps.title: Sparse polynomials and factor reversal
steps.note: Separate persistent reciprocal factors from the nonreciprocal part and use coefficient sparsity to restrict possible factorizations.

steps.title: Trinomials
steps.note: The polynomials xⁿ−x−1 realize Sₙ in every degree at least two. Modular reductions give certificates for individual examples; inertia gives a uniform proof.

steps.title: Eulerian polynomials
steps.note: Derive reciprocal symmetry from descent statistics, apply Eisenstein after a shift at prime indices, and compute the Galois group in a quartic example.

steps.title: Fekete polynomials
steps.note: Quadratic characters impose rational factors and reciprocal symmetry. Trace polynomials relate irreducibility and Galois groups to special values and square classes.

steps.title: Hermite, Bessel, and Legendre polynomials
steps.note: Study the factorization problems of Hermite, Bessel, and Legendre polynomials through parity reduction and coefficient products, accounting for the normalization of each family.

steps.title: Ehrhart polynomials
steps.note: Compare lattice-point counting with factorization and Galois groups.

steps.title: Exercise
steps.note: State the normalization, the ambient permutation group, a proved result, and an unresolved question with its source and stated range.

routes.title: Taylor polynomials and Katz–Rivin questions
routes.audience: Readers with a background in Galois theory
routes.goal: Distinguish arbitrary coefficient constructions from fixed arithmetic families.
routes.checkpoint: Explain why a nonconvergent prescribed sequence does not settle the rational-function convergence question.

steps.title: Classical examples
steps.note: Compare the exponential and geometric series.

steps.title: Frequency questions and arithmetic families
steps.note: Read the prescription theorem, the binomial and Catalan results, and the remaining questions. These results retain their preprint status.

steps.title: Construction by specialization
steps.note: Follow the use of generic groups and Hilbert irreducibility.

steps.title: Arithmetic methods
steps.note: Use valuations and inertia to study a fixed coefficient family.

steps.title: Exercise
steps.note: Explain why a nonconvergent prescribed sequence does not settle the rational-function convergence question.

routes.title: Models and asymptotic regimes for random polynomials
routes.audience: Researchers reading counting and random-polynomial papers
routes.goal: Specify the asymptotic parameter, coefficient law, conditioning, and analytic hypotheses.
routes.checkpoint: Explain why a fixed-degree height theorem does not imply a growing-degree fair-sign theorem.

steps.title: Height bounds for exceptional Galois groups
steps.note: As coefficient height grows at fixed degree, almost all integer polynomials have full symmetric group. Study the exceptional counts and the restrictions from reciprocal symmetry.

steps.title: Random polynomials: models and methods
steps.note: Specify the coefficient law and limiting parameter, then distinguish irreducibility, alternating-group containment, and full symmetric-group conclusions.

steps.title: Littlewood polynomials
steps.note: Independent sign coefficients impose congruence constraints. The examples also show why reduction modulo two does not resolve the all-degree probabilistic problem.

steps.title: Random reciprocal polynomials of growing degree
steps.note: A separable reciprocal polynomial of even degree has inverse root pairs and a signed-permutation group. Study the independent-coefficient model through its trace polynomial.

steps.title: Characteristic polynomials of random matrices
steps.note: Independent matrix entries give dependent characteristic-polynomial coefficients. Local rank estimates provide input specific to these models.

steps.title: Exercise
steps.note: Explain why a fixed-degree height theorem does not imply a growing-degree fair-sign theorem.

routes.title: From generic families to arithmetic specializations
routes.audience: Graduate readers interested in arithmetic geometry and inverse Galois theory
routes.goal: Relate generic monodromy to arithmetic specialization, with the quantifiers in each conclusion stated explicitly.
routes.checkpoint: Distinguish infinitely many good specializations, all but finitely many, density one, and an infinite tower.

steps.title: Critical points and polynomial monodromy
steps.note: Use critical points and critical values to determine the generic group, then compare it with the groups of four rational fibers in a cubic example.

steps.title: Specialization and Hilbert irreducibility
steps.note: Specialize a polynomial over a rational function field and study the exceptional parameter values.

steps.title: Inverse Galois theory and generic polynomials
steps.note: Construct polynomials with prescribed groups and distinguish individual realizations, regular families, and universal parametrizations.

steps.title: Composition, iteration, and arboreal groups
steps.note: Study repeated polynomial composition through extension towers and rooted trees. Distinguish stability from maximality of the Galois action.

steps.title: Generalized Laguerre polynomials
steps.note: Use factorial coefficient products to relate local slopes to Galois-group constraints. Distinguish fixed parameter with increasing degree from fixed degree with varying parameter.

steps.title: Exercise
steps.note: Distinguish infinitely many good specializations, all but finitely many, density one, and an infinite tower.

routes.title: Exact computation and certificates
routes.audience: Readers using computer algebra in proofs
routes.goal: Study factorization and Galois-group algorithms and identify the steps that certify their outputs.
routes.checkpoint: Record the exact input, software version, field, factorization or resolvent certificate, and certification step.

steps.title: Irreducibility over finite fields
steps.note: Use Frobenius-power tests to certify irreducibility, count irreducibles, and distinguish irreducible from primitive polynomials.

steps.title: Polynomial factorization algorithms
steps.note: Study Frobenius and linear algebra in finite-field factorization, followed by p-adic lifting and lattice reduction for factorization over the rationals.

steps.title: Resolvents and subgroup tests
steps.note: A resolvent records the group action on selected expressions in the roots. Rational factors can detect an invariant partition or restrict the group to a smaller subgroup.

steps.title: Algorithms for Galois groups
steps.note: Combine exact arithmetic, subgroup constraints, and certification, recording the inputs and certificates needed to reproduce the proof.

steps.title: Sparse input
steps.note: Specify the factor degree, input encoding, and output representation.

steps.title: Exercise
steps.note: Record the exact input, software version, field, factorization or resolvent certificate, and certification step.

methods.question: Is a given polynomial irreducible over Q?
methods.signal: Factorization modulo one or more small primes
methods.method: Degree-preserving reduction and intersection of possible factor degrees
methods.output: An irreducibility certificate if every proper factor degree is excluded
methods.boundary: An irreducible polynomial need not have an irreducible reduction at any prime.
methods.input: Factorization modulo one or more small primes

methods.question: Can coefficient divisibility prove irreducibility?
methods.signal: One prime divides all lower coefficients, or the valuations have a simple pattern
methods.output: Irreducibility over a local field, hence over Q, or restrictions on factor degrees
methods.boundary: Failure of a sufficient criterion does not imply reducibility.
methods.input: One prime divides all lower coefficients, or the valuations have a simple pattern

methods.question: Can several local tests work together?
methods.signal: Different primes exclude different factor degrees
methods.output: Irreducibility when the permitted proper factor degrees have empty intersection
methods.boundary: The degree restrictions from different primes may still have a common proper degree.
methods.input: Different primes exclude different factor degrees

methods.question: Can root sizes rule out factors?
methods.signal: A monic integer polynomial satisfying Perron's coefficient inequality, or a root bound at a prime-valued argument
methods.method: Perron's criterion and archimedean factor bounds
methods.output: Irreducibility from root location and integral constant terms or factor evaluations
methods.boundary: Perron's test needs monicity and a nonzero constant term; the displayed bounds are strict.
methods.input: A monic integer polynomial satisfying Perron's coefficient inequality, or a root bound at a prime-valued argument

methods.question: Can integer evaluations rule out every factor?
methods.signal: Many distinct integer arguments with small nonzero values, or at least 2n+1 unit or prime values for a primitive degree-n polynomial
methods.method: Schur unit-value arguments, Pólya interpolation, and prime-value counting
methods.output: An irreducibility certificate from restrictions on the values of possible integral factors
methods.boundary: Use the stated degree-dependent threshold and distinct arguments; one prime value alone is insufficient.
methods.input: Many distinct integer arguments with small nonzero values, or at least 2n+1 unit or prime values for a primitive degree-n polynomial

methods.question: Is a composition or binomial irreducible?
methods.signal: An irreducible outer polynomial F, a nonconstant inner polynomial g, or a binomial in characteristic zero
methods.method: Capelli root-field reduction and the exact binomial power criterion
methods.output: A lower-degree irreducibility question over a root field; for binomials, necessary and sufficient power exclusions
methods.boundary: Irreducibility of both inputs is insufficient. Binomials with exponent divisible by 4 require the exceptional negative-four-times-a-fourth-power exclusion.
methods.input: An irreducible outer polynomial F, a nonconstant inner polynomial g, or a binomial in characteristic zero

methods.question: What happens when a sparse polynomial has a large gap?
methods.signal: A family x^N c(x^{-1})+d(x) with fixed c and d
methods.output: Irreducibility of a specified nonreciprocal part for sufficiently large N
methods.boundary: The conclusion requires separate treatment of reciprocal factors and Capellian exceptions.
methods.input: A family x^N c(x^{-1})+d(x) with fixed c and d

methods.question: Which permutations occur in the Galois group?
methods.signal: Squarefree factorization at a prime of good reduction
methods.output: An element of the specified cycle type
methods.boundary: Use squarefree reduction at good primes. Failure to observe a cycle type at the tested primes does not exclude it from the group.
methods.input: Squarefree factorization at a prime of good reduction

methods.question: When do cycle types force A_n or S_n?
methods.signal: Transitivity, primitivity, and an appropriate prime cycle or transposition
methods.output: A proved group containment or equality
methods.boundary: A transitive subgroup containing a transposition need not be \(S_n\).
methods.input: Transitivity, primitivity, and an appropriate prime cycle or transposition

methods.question: How can A_n be distinguished from S_n?
methods.signal: A separable degree-n polynomial in characteristic different from 2, with containment of A_n already proved
methods.method: Discriminant square class or an odd permutation
methods.boundary: A nonsquare discriminant alone does not prove \(S_n\).
methods.input: A separable degree-n polynomial in characteristic different from 2, with containment of A_n already proved

methods.question: Does a root symmetry force a smaller ambient group?
methods.output: A wreath-product or other structural upper bound
methods.boundary: Root symmetry can exclude the full symmetric group \(S_n\).

methods.question: How can remaining candidate groups be separated?
methods.signal: Several subgroups fit the observed Frobenius types
methods.method: Resolvents, relative invariants, and subgroup descent
methods.output: Additional exact constraints or a certified group
methods.boundary: A numerical approximation or a candidate group alone does not certify the result.
methods.input: Several subgroups fit the observed Frobenius types

methods.question: Do generic results survive parameter specialization?
methods.signal: An irreducible separable family over K(t), with K Hilbertian (for example, K=Q)
methods.method: Hilbert irreducibility and specialized geometric criteria
methods.output: Irreducible specializations, with the exceptional set described under the stated hypotheses
methods.boundary: Infinitely many, density one, and all but finitely many are different conclusions.
methods.input: An irreducible separable family over K(t), with K Hilbertian (for example, K=Q)

methods.question: Are all iterates irreducible?
methods.signal: A polynomial f and the tower of its iterates
methods.method: Capelli-type steps, critical orbits, and arboreal groups
methods.output: Irreducibility at finitely many levels or at every level, under the corresponding hypotheses
methods.boundary: Specializing each finite level does not select one specialization valid at every level.
methods.input: A polynomial f and the tower of its iterates

methods.question: Can an irreducible polynomial over F_q be constructed or certified?
methods.signal: Specified degree and possibly prescribed coefficients
methods.method: Frobenius congruences, gcd tests, and finite-field constructions
methods.output: A finite-field irreducibility certificate or an existence theorem
methods.boundary: Primitive is stronger than irreducible; an irreducible degree-n polynomial has cyclic splitting-field group.
methods.input: Specified degree and possibly prescribed coefficients

methods.question: Is a multivariate polynomial absolutely irreducible?
methods.signal: Sparse exponent support or an effective specialization problem
methods.output: Irreducibility after extending the coefficient field to an algebraic closure
methods.boundary: Exclude monomial factors; this differs from ordinary irreducibility over the ground field.
methods.input: Sparse exponent support or an effective specialization problem

methods.question: Which coefficient models does a probabilistic theorem cover?
methods.signal: A coefficient law and a specified limiting parameter
methods.method: Local mixing, sieve methods, and factor exclusion
methods.output: A probability estimate for the exact model in the theorem
methods.boundary: State the conditioning, the distinction between \(A_n\) and \(S_n\), and any RH or GRH hypothesis.
methods.input: A coefficient law and a specified limiting parameter

methods.question: What is the generic Galois group of F(X)−T?
methods.signal: A polynomial of degree n≥2 in characteristic zero, with simple critical points and pairwise distinct critical values
methods.input: A polynomial of degree n≥2 in characteristic zero, with simple critical points and pairwise distinct critical values
methods.method: Morse criterion: finite branch inertia generates transpositions
methods.output: Geometric and arithmetic group \(S_n\); a regular splitting field
methods.boundary: A full generic group does not determine every rational fiber. Check specialization separately.

methods.question: Does a sparse polynomial have a factor of bounded degree?
methods.input: Sparse coefficients and binary-encoded exponents over a number field
methods.method: Separate cyclotomic factors and use exponent gaps
methods.output: All monic irreducible factors of degree at most d, with multiplicities
methods.boundary: The running time is polynomial in d, not in log d; dense full output can be too large.
